program_plain: World: a 64x64 lattice of cells (wrap-around edges, 8 neighbours each). Cells have 3 types (bare ground, dark daisy, light daisy; random start). Each cell's local temperature is set by incoming sunlight and the albedo of its own type and its neighbours (dark absorbs more). Rules each step: a daisy dies with probability 0.3; a bare cell next to a daisy becomes that daisy type with probability given by a growth curve that peaks at 22.5 C; sunlight increases slowly over the run.
standard_name: Spatial Daisyworld: patchy coexistence of black/white daisies with temperature regulation and hysteresis under luminosity ramp
citations: Wood, Ackland, Dyke, Williams, Lenton 2008, Reviews of Geophysics 46 RG1001 - review of Daisyworld incl. 2-D spatial versions (almost perfect regulator; von Bloh 1997, Ackland 2003)
Adams et al. 2003, J. Theor. Biol. 223:505-513 - One-dimensional daisyworld: heat diffusion destabilises coexistence, striped black/white domains emerge
A Spatial Daisyworld Model (Springer/ACM chapter, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-71552-5_20) - CA-like spatial Daisyworld, finite luminosity rate induces new hysteresis
Watson & Lovelock 1983 - original Daisyworld (title seen in reference list only; venue not verified from results)

full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is the spatial Daisyworld model of Watson and Lovelock, run as a stochastic cellular automaton with a sunlight ramp.

**1. Model family.** It is a Daisyworld-type model, which sits between reaction-diffusion/ecological models and cellular automata. It has a growth curve peaking at 22.5 °C, two albedo types (dark and light daisies) and bare ground, with temperature feedback. Here the temperature is local, set by the cell's own albedo and its neighbours' albedo. The sunlight (luminosity) is ramped up over the run.

**2. The specific behaviour.** The observed features are:
- Both daisy types and bare ground survive together (3 types).
- Like cells cluster in space (high Moran's I).
- One type takes up much of the lattice.

These are the standard outcomes of spatial Daisyworld:
- **Patchy coexistence.** The earliest clear source I found is the one-dimensional model by Adams et al. (2003). Its abstract reports that adding heat diffusion destabilises the two-daisy coexistence state. A striped pattern of blocks of all-black or all-white daisies emerges. The Wood et al. review also cites von Bloh et al. (1997) and Ackland et al. (2003) for 2-D versions. I did not open either paper; the review text only names them in passing.
- **Temperature regulation under rising luminosity.** The review notes that the 2-D Daisyworld is an almost perfect temperature regulator.
- **Cellular-automaton version with a finite luminosity ramp.** A recent paper describes a simple spatial implementation of the classic Daisyworld model, similar to a cellular automaton. It reports that colonisation is difficult and that, coupled to a finite velocity of the variation of luminosity of the sun, it induces new hysteresis cycles.
- **Fast-ramp variant.** Rate-dependent collapse under faster forcing is covered by the arXiv paper "Rate-induced biosphere collapse in the Daisyworld model" (arXiv 2410.00043). I only saw its title and reference list, not its abstract or text. Its abstract, as quoted in the Grokipedia summary, says abrupt luminosity increases can crash both daisy populations at once. That is a zero-dimensional result, so it supports the fast-ramp variant only indirectly.

**3. Citations checked against search results.**
- Wood, Ackland, Dyke, Williams & Lenton (2008), "Daisyworld: A review", *Reviews of Geophysics* 46, RG1001, doi:10.1029/2006RG000217. Title, authors, year and venue all match the York and Wiley pages.
- Adams, Carr, Kaltz, Lenton? I could not confirm the full author list from the results. I can confirm it is "One-dimensional daisyworld", *J. Theor. Biol.* 223 (2003) 505–513, so I cite it without authors.
- Watson & Lovelock (1983), "Biological homeostasis of the global environment: the parable of Daisyworld". Its title appears in an arXiv reference list; I did not verify the venue (*Tellus B*) from the results, and it is from memory.
- "A Spatial Daisyworld Model" (ACM/Springer chapter, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-71552-5_20). The authors and year were not shown in the results.

**4. Differences.** Several details are specific to this rule system:
- The 8-neighbour local-albedo temperature.
- The 0.3 death rate.
- A growth curve that peaks at 22.5 °C.
- The random start.

These look like parameter choices and should not change the qualitative behaviour. I did not find a source for the exact combination of cell-type entropy and largest-domain statistics. That is a measurement choice rather than a new phenomenon.

**5. Confidence: medium.** The model class and its qualitative behaviour are well documented. I could not confirm that any source matches the exact stochastic CA parameters, so the reported numbers are not compared quantitatively.
